summary: Defines what XMPP addresses look like, including names that use characters beyond plain ASCII, such as letters from other writing systems. It relies on the PRECIS approach to internationalized strings. It replaces RFC 6122.

plainLanguage.summary:
An XMPP address has up to three parts: an optional account name, a required server name, and an optional resource that identifies one of several connections or sessions on that account. The format has to cope with letters and symbols from any writing system.

This RFC replaces the old stringprep rules with the newer PRECIS framework, which says how such a string should be prepared before use, what characters are forbidden, and how two of them should be compared. The server name follows the internationalized domain name rules.

subtitle: What an XMPP address looks like, and how letters from other writing systems are allowed in it.

tldr.problem: The XMPP address format was built on stringprep, the technology used for internationalized domain names. That technology has been retired, so the address rules needed a replacement that still handles characters outside the ASCII range.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC keeps the shape of an address but rebuilds the rules on PRECIS, the IETF framework for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized strings, and on IDNA2008 for the domain part. Each of the three parts of an address gets its own profile and its own excluded characters.
tldr.outcome: Addresses can hold letters from any writing system, and the rules say exactly how to compare two addresses for equality. There is no guarantee of strict backward compatibility, so operators are advised to test before migrating. The RFC obsoletes RFC 6122 and has since been updated by RFC 9844.

facts.label: Maximum length of a whole address

today: RFC 7622 is a Proposed Standard from September 2015. It obsoletes RFC 6122 and has since been updated by RFC 9844. The document notes that the stringprep profiles it replaces have been marked as not current in the registry, and that because PRECIS works from Unicode properties rather than a fixed table, operators are advised to test before migrating accounts.

sections.title: Why the Address Format Needed Rewriting
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol is an application profile of XML for streaming XML data in close to real time between any two or more network-aware entities. The address format for XMPP entities was first developed in the Jabber open-source community in 1999, described by an extension in 2002, and then defined canonically by RFC 3920 in 2004 and RFC 6122 in 2011.

Those specifications used stringprep for the preparation and comparison of non-ASCII characters. Following the movement of internationalized domain names away from stringprep, this document defines the XMPP address format in a way that no longer depends on stringprep. Instead it builds on the internationalization framework defined by the IETF's PRECIS working group in RFC 7564.

Although every attempt has been made to ensure that the characters allowed in Jabber Identifiers under stringprep are still allowed and handled the same way under PRECIS, there is no guarantee of strict backward compatibility. The reasons are changes in Unicode and the fact that PRECIS handling is based on Unicode properties rather than a hardcoded table of characters. Because previously valid addresses might no longer be valid, and previously invalid ones might now be valid, operators of XMPP services are advised to perform careful testing before migrating accounts and other data.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules for handling foreign characters came from a technology that has since been withdrawn. The replacement is the same family of rules that now governs internationalized domain names, which is a better fit for a chat address than domain rules ever were.

sections.title: The Shape of an XMPP Address
sections.content:
An XMPP entity is anything that can communicate using XMPP. For historical reasons the network address of an XMPP entity is called a JID. A valid JID is a string of Unicode code points encoded in UTF-8, structured as an ordered sequence of localpart, domainpart and resourcepart, where the first two parts are demarcated by the at sign and the last two by the solidus. The example given is the address of a user on a balcony.

The syntax is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form. A JID is an optional localpart, then the at sign, then a domainpart, then optionally the solidus and a resourcepart. The localpart is one to 1023 userbytes, where a userbyte is a byte used to represent a UTF-8 encoded Unicode code point that can be contained in a string conforming to the UsernameCaseMapped profile of the PRECIS IdentifierClass. The domainpart is an IP literal, an IPv4 address, or an ifqdn, where the first two rules come from the URI and IP-literal specifications and the first-match-wins algorithm of the URI specification applies to the matching. The ifqdn is one to 1023 domainbytes, where a domainbyte is a byte used to represent a UTF-8 encoded Unicode code point that can be contained in a string conforming to the internationalized domain name framework. The resourcepart is one to 1023 opaquebytes, where an opaquebyte is a byte representing a UTF-8 encoded Unicode code point that can be contained in a string conforming to the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass.

The formal syntax does not capture all the rules and restrictions that apply, which are described in the rest of the document. Each allowable portion of a JID is 1 to 1023 octets in length, giving a maximum total size, including the two separator characters, of 3071 octets. The limits are on octets, not characters, because UTF-8 encoding can produce more than one octet per character. When dividing an address into its parts, an implementation needs to match the separator characters before applying any transformation algorithm, which might decompose certain Unicode code points into the separator characters.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is up to three pieces joined by an at sign and a slash. The whole thing fits in about three thousand bytes, and each piece in a thousand. The counts are in bytes, so a letter from a non-Latin script uses more than one.

sections.title: The Domainpart
sections.content:
The domainpart is what remains after two parsing steps. First, remove any portion from the first solidus to the end of the string, if there is a solidus. Then remove any portion from the beginning of the string to the first at sign, if there is one. The order matters, as the examples show.

The domainpart is the primary identifier and is the only required element of a JID, since a mere domainpart is a valid JID. It typically identifies the home server that clients connect to for routing and data management, but it does not have to identify an entity that provides core server functionality: a domainpart can identify a multi-user chat service, a publish-subscribe service or a user directory. The domainpart of every XMPP service must be a fully qualified domain name, an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or an unqualified hostname that is resolvable on a local network. The RFC notes that the term fully qualified domain name is not well defined, and that older specifications ought not to be read as limiting such a name to the ASCII range, since a fully qualified domain name can contain U-labels.

Domainparts that are IP addresses might not be accepted by other services for server-to-server communication, and unqualified hostnames cannot be used on public networks because they resolve only on a local network.

If the domainpart ends with a character that is considered a label separator, that character must be stripped before the address is used for routing a stanza, comparing it against another address, or constructing a URI. It must be stripped before any other canonicalization step is taken.

The preparation rules require that a string contain only Unicode code points allowed in NR-LDH labels or U-labels, which implies it must not include A-labels, and that each A-label be converted to a U-label during preparation. The string must also be encoded as UTF-8. Enforcement applies the same preparation and then the normalization, case-mapping and width-mapping rules of the IDNA2008 specification, and the order in which those rules apply differs from the order used for the localpart and the resourcepart. Comparison prepares and enforces each of two strings and then treats them as equivalent if they are an exact octet-for-octet match. After all normalization, conversion, mapping and encoding, a domainpart must not be zero octets long and must not be more than 1023 octets long.
sections.plainLanguage: The server name is the part that has to be there. It follows the same rules as an internationalized domain name, and the trailing dot is removed before the address is used. Two addresses are the same only if they match byte for byte after all of that.

sections.title: The Localpart and the Resourcepart
sections.content:
The localpart is an optional identifier placed before the domainpart and separated from it by the at sign. It typically identifies the entity requesting and using network access provided by a server, that is, a local account, although it can also represent other kinds of entity such as a chatroom. The entity it represents is addressed within the context of a specific domain. The localpart must not be zero octets in length and must not be more than 1023 octets long, after any normalization and mapping and UTF-8 encoding. It is an instance of the UsernameCaseMapped profile of the PRECIS IdentifierClass, and the rules of that specification must be applied to it. The RFC notes that XMPP uses SASL for authentication, and that some SASL mechanisms currently use SASLprep for handling usernames and passwords, with a likely future transition to PRECIS-based handling.

Several characters are explicitly disallowed in localparts even though the PRECIS base class and the UsernameCaseMapped profile allow them: the quotation mark, the ampersand, the apostrophe, the solidus, the colon, the less-than sign, the greater-than sign and the commercial at sign. An XMPP-specific method of escaping those characters, along with the ASCII space, has been defined in the JID Escaping extension.

The resourcepart is an optional identifier placed after the domainpart and separated from it by the solidus. It can modify either a full address or a bare domainpart. It typically identifies a specific connection, such as a device or a location, or an object such as an occupant in a multi-user chatroom, belonging to the entity associated with the localpart.

Entities should consider resourceparts to be opaque strings and should not impute meaning to any given one. Using the solidus as a separator does not imply that XMPP addresses are hierarchical in the way that HTTP URIs are, so an address of the form localpart at domainpart, slash, foo, slash, bar does not identify a resource bar that exists below a resource foo. The at sign is allowed in the resourcepart and is often used as the handle shown in XMPP chatrooms, so the address for a room occupant at a chatroom includes the occupant's handle. However, chatroom services do not necessarily check such an asserted handle against the occupant's real JID.

The resourcepart must not be zero octets in length and must not be more than 1023 octets long, after normalization and encoding. It is an instance of the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass, and the rules of that specification must be applied to it. In some contexts it may be appropriate to apply more restrictive rules, for example the nickname rules in the multi-user chat extension, but the application of more restrictive rules is out of scope for resourceparts in general and belongs in the specifications for the relevant extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The account name before the at sign follows a profile that forbids a handful of punctuation characters. The part after the slash is treated as an opaque label: nothing is implied by its shape, and a chatroom handle in it is only a claim.

sections.title: What Legal Addresses Look Like
sections.content:
The RFC gives a table of fifteen example addresses and comments on the ones that teach something.

Examples 6 and 7 are two addresses that differ only in the third character of the account name, where one uses the German esszett and the other two lower-case letters. Although the two characters can mostly be used interchangeably in German, the localparts are different, and a server would need a registration policy that disallows one of them if the other is registered.

Examples 9, 10 and 11 use the three Greek forms of sigma. Case-mapping the capital sigma to lower case during comparison would make the addresses in examples 9 and 10 match, but because the PRECIS mapping rules do not account for the special status of the Greek small letter final sigma, the addresses in examples 9 and 11, or 10 and 11, would not match.

Example 12 uses a symbol character, the black chess king, which the PRECIS FreeformClass allows and which can therefore be used in a resourcepart. Examples 14 and 15 are addresses consisting of a domainpart and a resourcepart, which are rarely seen in the wild but are allowed. Example 15 illustrates the need for the careful extraction of the domainpart described earlier, because the resourcepart itself contains an at sign.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that two addresses can look identical to a person and still be different to a computer. A German sharp s and two letters are not the same, and the three Greek forms of sigma do not all match each other.

sections.title: Who Enforces the Rules
sections.content:
Enforcement applies to complete addresses and to parts of addresses. To make this practical the RFC defines the concepts of a JID slot, a localpart slot and a resourcepart slot, mirroring the idea of a domain name slot in the internationalized domain name specifications. A JID slot is an XML element or attribute explicitly designated for carrying a complete JID, a localpart slot for carrying the localpart, and a resourcepart slot for carrying the resourcepart.

A server is responsible for enforcing the address format rules when it receives protocol elements from clients where the server is expected to handle those elements directly or to use them for routing a stanza to another domain or delivering it to a local entity. The to attribute on XML stanzas is an example of a JID slot used for routing outbound stanzas, and the resource child of the bind element is an example of a resourcepart slot used for binding a resource to an account. The jid attribute of the roster item element is an example from the roster management specification.

A server is not responsible for enforcing the rules when the protocol elements are intended for communication among other entities, typically inside the payload of a stanza that the server is merely routing. The initiator attribute in the Jingle extension and the nick attribute in the multi-user chat extension are given as examples. In such cases the entities involved should enforce the rules themselves rather than depend on the server, and client implementers need to understand that not enforcing them can lead to a degraded user experience or to security vulnerabilities. When an add-on service handles a stanza directly, it ought to enforce the rules as well, as defined in the relevant specification for that kind of service.
sections.plainLanguage: A server checks the addresses it uses for routing, because it is the one making a routing decision. It does not police the addresses buried inside a message, since it is only passing those along; the participants in the conversation are expected to check them for themselves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the PRECIS framework apply to the IdentifierClass and FreeformClass base string classes used here for localparts and resourceparts, and those of the internationalized domain name framework apply to the domainparts. The security considerations of the Unicode security guidance apply to the use of Unicode characters in XMPP addresses.

There are two forms of address spoofing: forging and mimicking. Address forging occurs when an entity is able to generate an XML stanza whose from address does not correspond to the account credentials with which the entity authenticated, or to an authorization identity provided during negotiation of SASL authentication. For example, forging occurs if an entity that authenticated as one address is able to send stanzas from another address on a different domain.

Forging is difficult in XMPP systems, given the requirement for sending servers to stamp from addresses and for receiving servers to verify sending domains through server-to-server authentication. It is nevertheless possible if a poorly implemented server ignores the requirement for stamping the from address, which would let any entity authenticated with the server send stanzas from any localpart at that server's domain, or if an actively malicious server generates stanzas on behalf of any registered account it hosts. An entity outside the security perimeter of a server therefore cannot reliably distinguish between addresses at that server and can authenticate only the domainpart with any level of assurance. The specification defines no methods for discovering or counteracting such servers, but end-to-end authentication or signing of stanzas could help, because it would require the rogue server to generate false credentials for signing or encryption as well as modify from addresses.

Address mimicking occurs when an entity provides legitimate credentials for an account whose address appears to a human to be the same as another address. Because many characters are visually similar, it is relatively easy to mimic addresses. The localpart ju1iet, using the Arabic numeral one as the third character, might appear the same as juliet, using a lower-case L.

There is no straightforward solution to the problem of visually similar characters, and neither IDNA nor PRECIS attempts to define one. As a result, all three parts of an address could contain such characters, with several consequences. A domainpart is always part of an entity's address, and a user might authorize a malicious entity at a fake server to view presence information, or join chatrooms at a fake chat service. A localpart is often the user name of an instant messaging user, and a user entering a single internationalized localpart could access another user's account information or reach a hidden chatroom. A resourcepart is often the name for a connected resource or a chatroom nickname, and two confusable resources could be bound at the same time to the same account, leading to inconsistent authorization decisions, or a user could send a private message to someone other than the intended recipient.

XMPP services and clients are strongly encouraged to define and implement consistent policies regarding the registration, storage and presentation of visually similar characters, and service providers and implementers are strongly encouraged to apply the policies recommended in the PRECIS specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attacks matter here. One is sending a message that claims to come from an address you did not log in as. The other is using a different address that looks the same to a person, such as a digit one where a letter L would look the same. The second has no general fix, so the RFC asks servers and clients to agree on a consistent policy.

viz.caption: The address syntax, as printed in the RFC

data.title: JID syntax
data.code:
jid          = [ localpart "@" ] domainpart [ "/" resourcepart ]
localpart    = 1*1023(userbyte)
domainpart   = IP-literal / IPv4address / ifqdn
ifqdn        = 1*1023(domainbyte)
resourcepart = 1*1023(opaquebyte)

viz.caption: The three parts of an XMPP address
What each part of an address is for

items.title: Localpart
items.text: The part before the at sign. Usually the account name, but it can also name a chatroom.

items.title: Domainpart
items.text: The part between the at sign and the slash. Usually the home server, but it can name any service.

items.title: Resourcepart
items.text: The part after the slash. Usually a device, a location, or an occupant of a chatroom.

items.title: Whole address
items.text: At most 3071 octets, counting the two separator characters.

viz.caption: The characters excluded from the localpart

items.label: Solidus
items.desc: Excluded from localparts, since it separates the domainpart from the resourcepart.

items.label: Commercial at
items.desc: Excluded from localparts, since it separates the localpart from the domainpart.

viz.caption: A sample of legal addresses, from the table in the RFC

data.title: Sample of legal JIDs
data.code:
juliet@example.com            a bare JID
juliet@example.com/foo        a full JID
juliet@example.com/foo bar    a space in the resourcepart
juliet@example.com/foo@bar    an at sign in the resourcepart
foo\20bar@example.com         a space in the localpart, escaped
fußball@example.com           LATIN SMALL LETTER SHARP S in the localpart
π@example.com                 GREEK SMALL LETTER PI as the localpart
king@example.com/♔           a black chess king in the resourcepart
example.com                   a domainpart on its own
a.example.com/b@example.net   a domainpart, then a resourcepart with an at sign

viz.caption: The two ways an XMPP address can be abused

items.title: Forging
items.text: Sending a message with a from address that is not the one you signed in as. Stamping from addresses and verifying sending domains make it hard, but a poorly implemented or rogue server can still do it.

items.title: Mimicking
items.text: Using a different account whose address looks the same to a person, for example ju1iet with a digit one in place of juliet with a lower-case L.

items.title: No general fix
items.text: Neither the domain name rules nor PRECIS attempt to solve the problem of visually similar characters.

items.title: Consistent policies
items.text: Services and clients are strongly encouraged to define and implement consistent policies for registering, storing and showing visually similar characters.
